summary: This RFC extends WebDAV so clients can efficiently synchronize the contents of a collection, without re-fetching everything.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of copying a whole folder again, you ask what changed since last time and only get that.

questions: how does webdav sync token work
subtitle: A token-based report that lets WebDAV clients ask only what changed in a collection since last time.

tldr.problem: WebDAV clients that cache a collection had to list every member with its ETag through PROPFIND to find changes, and that response grows with the size of the collection.
tldr.mechanism: A new DAV:sync-collection report takes a synchronization token and returns only the member URLs added, changed or removed since that token, plus a fresh token. A new DAV:sync-token property exposes the current token.
tldr.outcome: Clients send an empty token for the first full listing and the last token afterwards. Servers may invalidate old tokens, in which case the client falls back to a full sync.

facts.label: Token format
facts.value: Any valid URI, opaque to the client

today: RFC 6578 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text does not name particular products or deployments, so this page does not either.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
WebDAV defines collections, which are hierarchical groupings of resources on an HTTP server. A client that caches resources needs to detect what changed. Before this RFC the way was a PROPFIND on the collection that lists every member with its DAV:getetag value, so the client can see what was changed, added or deleted. That does not scale, because the XML response grows with the collection.

RFC 6578 adds a new report that returns only the member URLs that were added or deleted, or whose mapped resources changed, since a previous run of the report. It also adds a property on collections carrying a synchronization token that is guaranteed to change when the members or their resources change.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a whole folder every time is slow when the folder is big. This RFC lets you ask only what is new since your last look.

sections.title: How Token-Based Sync Works
sections.content:
Each time the report runs, the server gives the client a token representing the collection's state at that moment. The client presents the same token later and gets back only the new, changed and deleted items, along with a new token.

The first time, the client sends an empty token, and the server returns all member URLs. The client may instead do its first synchronization some other way, such as PROPFIND, SEARCH or the reports in CalDAV and CardDAV, and ask for the DAV:sync-token property to get a token to use later.

A server may keep only limited history. When a client sends an out-of-date token, the server returns an error and the client has to re-run the report with an empty token. Clients also need to be aware that changes can happen between the report and the later fetches of content, and can track this by comparing ETag values, using conditional requests, or repeating the sync until no changes come back.

The token itself is opaque to the client, but it MUST be a valid URI so it can be used in an If header. A simple implementation could append a change counter to a base URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket from your last visit tells the shopkeeper exactly where you left off. On your first visit you have no ticket, so you get the whole list.

sections.title: The sync-collection Report
sections.content:
The request is a REPORT whose request-URI MUST be a collection. The body is a DAV:sync-collection element that MUST contain one DAV:sync-token, one DAV:sync-level and one DAV:prop, and MAY contain a DAV:limit. The report is defined only for Depth: 0, and other values give a 400 (Bad Request). A server that implements it MUST list it in DAV:supported-report-set.

A successful response is a DAV:multistatus containing one DAV:sync-token and one DAV:response per member URL that was added, changed or removed. Each URL appears only once.

  • Changed or new members: the response has at least one DAV:propstat and no DAV:status.
  • Removed members: one DAV:status of 404 Not Found and no DAV:propstat.
  • Child collections that cannot sync: a 403 Forbidden status with a DAV:error holding DAV:supported-report or DAV:sync-traversal-supported.

The DAV:sync-level element is how clients scope the sync. A value of 1 reports immediate children, while infinite reports all members at any depth, provided child collections support the report. Tokens are not specific to a level.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand over the ticket and say how deep to look. The answer lists new and changed things with their details, and removed things marked as gone.

sections.title: What Counts as Changed or Removed
sections.content:
On an initial sync with an empty token, the server MUST return all member URLs of every type and MUST NOT return any removed ones.

A member URL MUST be reported as changed if it has been newly mapped into the collection since the token was issued, including through COPY, MOVE, BIND or REBIND. It MUST also be reported as changed if its resource's entity tag changed. If a mapping was removed and then recreated with the same URI, the URL is reported as changed, not removed. Changes to members of a collection do not necessarily alter the collection's own entity tag, so clients that need to follow all changes must use level infinite and cannot rely on repeated level 1 reports.

A member MUST be reported as removed if its mapping was removed and not remapped, for example by MOVE, UNBIND or REBIND. A member added and then removed between two reports MUST be reported as removed, so a client that added it learns of the removal. In an infinite report, when a collection is removed the server MUST NOT list its members, and clients MUST assume they are all gone.
sections.plainLanguage: If something was brought in, or its label changed, it goes on the changed list. If it left and did not come back, it goes on the gone list.

sections.title: Truncation, Limits and Invalid Tokens
sections.content:
A server MAY cut the result short, either to limit its own work or because the client set a DAV:limit. Then the response uses 207 (Multi-Status) and includes a DAV:response for the request-URI with status 507 (Insufficient Storage), which SHOULD carry a DAV:number-of-matches-within-limits error. The returned token MUST match the partial set of changes, so the client can page through the rest. Clients MUST handle the 507 status on the request-URI.

The RFC's worked example: a client holds token http://example.com/sync/10 and 15 changes have occurred. With no limit the server returns 15 responses and token sync/25. If the server limits to 10, it returns 10 responses and token sync/20, and the client asks again to get the remaining 5.

If the server cannot cut the result at or below the client's limit, it MUST fail with the DAV:number-of-matches-within-limits postcondition.

The DAV:valid-sync-token precondition requires that the token was previously returned for that collection. Servers MUST invalidate tokens only when absolutely necessary, for example when they cannot keep all change data (the RFC mentions maintaining up to 3 weeks of changes or up to 10,000 total changes) or after a change of implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: If the answer is too long, the shopkeeper hands you part of it with a new ticket, and you come back for the rest.

sections.title: The sync-token Property and If Header
sections.content:
The DAV:sync-token property has a value of any valid URI. It MUST be protected, because the server creates and controls it. It MUST be defined on every resource that supports the report and holds the token a report would return at that moment. It SHOULD NOT be returned by a PROPFIND allprop.

Servers MUST support using a sync-token as a state token in the WebDAV If header. That lets a client make a request succeed only if the collection is unchanged since its last sync. Because the token belongs to the collection and not the request target, the header uses the Resource_Tag form.

In the RFC's examples, a PUT of a new resource with a matching token returns 201 Created, while a MKCOL with a token that no longer matches returns 412 Precondition Failed.
sections.plainLanguage: You can also say do this only if nothing changed since my ticket. If somebody else changed things, the request is refused.

sections.title: Security and a Sample Client
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says only that the extension does not add security concerns beyond those already described for HTTP and WebDAV.

Appendix B sketches, as an example and not a required algorithm, how a client can sync the immediate children of a collection. It starts with an empty cache and no token, runs the report with an empty token and level 1 asking for DAV:getetag, then fetches each reported resource with GET and stores its path and ETag. On later runs it sends its stored token, deletes cached items reported with a 404, and fetches those that are new or whose ETag differs.

Appendix A adds a compatibility note. Older drafts used the Depth header instead of DAV:sync-level, so servers that want to work with such clients should use the Depth value when the element is missing.
sections.plainLanguage: A sample client just keeps a list of things with their version marks, and only downloads the ones that are new or have a different mark.
